text:
In Sangam poetry, each tinai (landscape) is tied to a way of life. Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
a) Kurinji – hunting and gathering
b) Mullai – cattle rearing
c) Marudam – farming
d) Palai – fishing and seafaring
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** The pair is correctly matched, so it is not the answer. Kurinji is the tinai of mountainous regions, and its main occupation is hunting and gathering (NCERT Class 6 Exploring Society, Ch 3, p. 57).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** The pair is correctly matched. Mullai is the tinai of grassland and forests, with cattle rearing (NCERT Class 6 Exploring Society, Ch 3, p. 57).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** The pair is correctly matched. Marudam is the tinai of fertile agricultural plains, with farming (NCERT Class 6 Exploring Society, Ch 3, p. 57).
**Option (d): Correct.** This pair is NOT correctly matched, so it is the answer. Palai is the tinai of arid, desert-like regions, and its occupation is **journeying and fighting**. Fishing and seafaring belong to **Neydal**, the coastal regions (NCERT Class 6 Exploring Society, Ch 3, p. 57).
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Kurinji, Mullai and Marudam are correctly matched; fishing and seafaring belong to Neydal, not Palai.

**Salient Features: The tinais and Sangam literature**
The five tinais of Sangam poetry are five landscapes, each associated with particular deities, lifestyles, moods or emotions (NCERT Class 6 Exploring Society, Ch 3, p. 57).
- **The word "sangam":** it is derived from the Sanskrit sangha, meaning "association" or "coming together", and here refers to an assembly of poets (NCERT Class 7 Exploring Society Part 1, Ch 6, PDF p. 14).
- **Three crowned kings:** the Sangam texts refer to three "crowned kings", the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas (NCERT Class 7 Exploring Society Part 1, Ch 6, PDF p. 14).
- **Manimekalai:** the heroine of this Tamil epic was the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi, and she became a Buddhist saint (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 6, PDF p. 105).
- **Thirukkural:** this moral work was written by Thiruvalluvar, a prominent poet of the Sangam age (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 6, PDF p. 105).

**Exam Fact:** Each stanza (kural) of the Thirukkural has only one and a half lines (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 6, PDF p. 105).

text:
The following statements relate to temples and art of early medieval India:
1. The Marthanda Sun temple in Kashmir was built by the Karkota dynasty.
2. Chikani paintings, encouraged by the Pallavas, were large frescoes on cave walls.
3. The tallest of the rock-carved statues outside Gwalior fort is that of Vrishabhanatha (Adinath), the first Jain Tirthankara.
4. The stone temple on Shankaracharya Hill near Srinagar is known as the Shankaracharya or Jyeshteshwara temple.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
a) 1, 2, 3 and 4
b) 1, 3 and 4 only
c) 2 and 3 only
d) 1 and 4 only
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** The famous Marthanda Sun temple in Kashmir is an important contribution of the **Karkota** dynasty (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 27).
**Statement 2: Incorrect.** Chikani paintings were encouraged by the **Rajputs**, not the Pallavas, and chikani means **miniature intricate drawings**, not large frescoes; they were done on the walls of palaces, temples and forts, and also on books (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 30).
**Statement 3: Correct.** Among the huge statues carved on the rocks outside Gwalior fort, the idol of Vrishabhanath (Adinath), the first Jain Tirthankara, is the tallest (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 29).
**Statement 4: Correct.** The stone temple on Shankaracharya Hill near Srinagar is known as the Shankaracharya temple or Jyeshteshwara temple (NCERT Class 7 Exploring Society Part 2, Ch 3, PDF p. 15).
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct, which is option (b). Option (a) includes the false 2, option (c) includes the false 2 and omits the true 1 and 4, and option (d) omits the true 3.
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** The Marthanda temple, the Gwalior Adinath statue and the Jyeshteshwara temple are correctly described; chikani paintings were Rajput miniatures.

**Salient Features: Kashmir and the Rajput age**
Both regions saw strong royal patronage of art and learning.
- **Karkota dynasty:** founded by Durlabhavardhana in 625 CE, its rulers were Sun-worshippers with their capital at Paraspore or Parihasapura (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 27).
- **Lalithaditya:** a notable Karkota ruler who came to power in 724 CE and gave ample encouragement to art and culture (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 27).
- **Gwalior fort:** called "the pearl among the Indian forts", it holds a two-storeyed palace built by Raja Mansingh for his queen Mriganayane (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 29).

**Exam Fact:** Shankaracharya Hill near Srinagar is also known as Takht-i-Sulaiman and was anciently called Gopadri Hill (NCERT Class 7 Exploring Society Part 2, Ch 3, PDF p. 14).

text:
Match List I with List II:

| List I (Author) | List II (Work) |
|---|---|
| A. Bhavabhuti | I. Karpuramanjari |
| B. Rajasekhara | II. Uttara Ramacharita |
| C. Dandi | III. Rajatarangini |
| D. Kalhana | IV. Dashakumaracharita |

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
a) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III
b) A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
c) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
d) A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
The correct pairing is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.
- **Bhavabhuti:** he wrote the "Uttara Ramacharita" (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, PDF p. 23; II PUC History, Ch 4.5, PDF p. 72). Bhavabhuti–II.
- **Rajasekhara:** his dramas include the "Karpuramanjari" (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, PDF p. 23). Rajasekhara–I.
- **Dandi:** he wrote the "Dashakumaracharita" (II PUC History, Ch 4.5, PDF p. 72; DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 19, PDF p. 28). Dandi–IV.
- **Kalhana:** he wrote the historical work "Rajatarangini" (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, PDF p. 23; II PUC History, Ch 1, PDF p. 22). Kalhana–III.

**Option (a): Incorrect.** It swaps Bhavabhuti and Dandi (A-IV, C-II).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** It swaps Dandi and Kalhana (C-III, D-IV).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** It swaps Bhavabhuti and Rajasekhara (A-I, B-II).
**Option (d): Correct.** It gives all four pairs correctly.
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Bhavabhuti wrote the Uttara Ramacharita, Rajasekhara the Karpuramanjari, Dandi the Dashakumaracharita and Kalhana the Rajatarangini.

**Salient Features: Sanskrit and regional literature, 8th to 12th centuries**
The same authors wrote several works, and many new works appeared under Rajput patronage.
- **Bhavabhuti:** he also wrote "Malati Madhava" and "Mahavira Charita" (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, PDF p. 23).
- **Rajasekhara:** his other drama is the "Balaramayana" (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, PDF p. 23).
- **Dandi:** he also wrote the "Kavyadarsha" (II PUC History, Ch 4.5, PDF p. 72).
- **Other works of the period:** the "Gita Govinda" of Jayadeva, the "Prithvirajaraso" of Chand Bardai and the "Kumarapalacharita" of Hemachandra (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 2, PDF p. 23).

**Exam Fact:** The Rajatarangini was among the works translated into Persian in Akbar's period (II PUC History, Ch 5.2, PDF p. 130).

text:
Which Delhi Sultanate ruler built the new capital city of Siri, a few kilometres from the earlier Qutb complex?
a) Alauddin Khalji
b) Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
c) Muhammad bin Tughlaq
d) Iltutmish
sol:
**Correct Option: (a)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Correct.** Alauddin Khalji built his capital at Siri, a few kilometres from the site around the Qutb; hardly anything of this city survives now (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 199). DSERT also records that he built a new fort in Delhi known as Siri (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 41).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, with Muhammad Tughlaq, built the huge palace-fortress complex called Tughlaqabad (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 200). Siri was the Khalji capital.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** Muhammad bin Tughlaq shared in the building of Tughlaqabad with Ghiyasuddin (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 200); Siri is Alauddin's.
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Iltutmish completed the Qutb Minar, which Qutbuddin Aibak had begun (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 39). Siri belongs to the Khalji period, after his time.
Hence the correct answer is option (a).

**Result:** Siri was Alauddin Khalji's capital; Tughlaqabad was built by Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad Tughlaq, and Iltutmish completed the Qutb Minar.

**Salient Features: Building in the Delhi Sultanate**
Satish Chandra notes that the Khalji period saw a lot of building activity (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 199).
- **The Alai Darwaza:** Alauddin added an entrance door to the Qutb, the Alai Darwaza, with arches of pleasing proportions and a dome that Satish Chandra describes as the first built on correct scientific lines (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 199).
- **An unfinished tower:** Alauddin planned a tower twice the height of the Qutb but did not live to complete it (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 199).
- **Arabesque:** the Turks avoided human and animal figures, using geometrical and floral designs combined with panels of Quranic verses; this combination was called arabesque (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 199).
- **Tughlaq buildings:** Tughlaqabad was surrounded by an artificial lake made by blocking the Yamuna, and sloping walls, called 'batter', became a striking feature of Tughlaq architecture (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 200).

**Exam Fact:** When the Mongols appeared in 1303, Alauddin Khalji, then campaigning against Chittor, rushed back and fortified himself at his new capital, Siri (Satish Chandra, History of Medieval India, PDF p. 103).

text:
Consider the following statements about the Wodeyars of Mysore:
1. Raja Wodeyar offered the Rajamudi crown to Goddess Chamundeshwari of Mysore.
2. Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar bore the titles Karnataka Kavichakravarti, Aprathima Veera and Thenkanaraja.
3. Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar captured Magadi, Madhugiri and Koratagere.
4. Raja Wodeyar revived the temples of Srirangapattana, Mysore and Melukote.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
a) 2 and 3 only
b) 1, 2 and 4 only
c) 2, 3 and 4 only
d) 1, 3 and 4 only
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Incorrect.** Raja Wodeyar offered the crown "Rajamudi" to **Lord Cheluvanarayana Swamy**, not to Goddess Chamundeshwari (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47). The Cheluvanarayanaswamy temple is at Melukote (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 3, PDF p. 38).
**Statement 2: Correct.** Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar had titles such as "Karnataka Kavichakravarthi", "Aprathima Veera" and "Thenkanaraja" (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).
**Statement 3: Correct.** He captured Magadi, Madhugiri, Koratagere and other places (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).
**Statement 4: Correct.** Raja Wodeyar revived the temples of Srirangapattana, Mysore and Melukote (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).
Statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct, which is option (c). Option (a) omits the true 4, option (b) includes the false 1 and omits the true 3, and option (d) includes the false 1 and omits the true 2.
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** The Rajamudi was offered to Cheluvanarayana Swamy, not Chamundeshwari; the other three statements are correct.

**Salient Features: Raja Wodeyar and Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar**
These two rulers turned a small paleyapattu into a strong Mysore kingdom.
- **Raja Wodeyar (1578–1617):** he is credited with expanding the small paleyapattu into a large Mysore; he captured Srirangapattana from the representative of Vijayanagara and made it his capital (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).
- **Dasara:** Raja Wodeyar started the Navaratri (Dasara) festival of the Mysore province at Srirangapattana (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).
- **Bangalore:** Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar (1673–1704) purchased Bangalore from the Mughal military general (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).
- **Administration:** Chikkadevaraja started a council of ministers, the Athara Kacheri, to help in administration (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).

**Exam Fact:** The postal system came into being in the time of Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar (DSERT Class 10 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 47).

text:
How many of the following statements about the Vaishnava acharyas and their traditions are correct?
1. Ramanujacharya learnt the Vedas and the Upanishads from Yadavaprakasha at Kanchi.
2. Saint Vadiraja reduced the period of the paryaya at Udupi to two weeks.
3. Ramanuja's Bhaktimarga has two elements, Prapatti and Acharyaabhimana.
4. Madhvacharya installed the idol of Krishna at Malpe and that of Balarama at Udupi.
a) Only one
b) Only two
c) Only three
d) All four
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** Ramanujacharya learnt the Vedas and the Upanishads from Yadavaprakasha in Kanchi, the famous educational centre of South India (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 3, PDF p. 37; II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 166).
**Statement 2: Incorrect.** Madhvacharya set up a system in which each pontiff worshipped Lord Krishna at Udupi for **two months** in rotation, and Saint Vadiraja later **extended** the paryaya to **two years**; he did not reduce it to two weeks (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 16, PDF p. 88).
**Statement 3: Correct.** Ramanuja's Bhaktimarga has two elements: Prapatti (absolute surrender to God) and Acharyaabhimana (subjugation to the guru) (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 167).
**Statement 4: Incorrect.** It reverses the two places. Madhvacharya installed **Krishna at Udupi** and **Balarama at Malpe** (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 167).
Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so two statements are correct, which is option (b).
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Vadiraja extended the paryaya to two years, and Krishna is at Udupi, Balarama at Malpe.

**Salient Features: Ramanuja and Madhva**
Both acharyas founded traditions that continue through their mathas.
- **Ramanuja's teaching:** his philosophy is called Vishishtadvaita and the religion he propagated Sri Vaishnavism, so his followers are called Sri Vaishnavites (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 3, PDF p. 38).
- **Ramanuja's works:** Vedanta Sangraha, Vedantasara, Vedanta Deepika, Shribhasya and Geethabhashya (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 3, PDF p. 38).
- **Madhva's names:** his earlier name was Vasudeva, and he was also known as Poorna Prajna and Ananda Teertha (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 167).
- **Other Madhva mathas:** apart from the Ashtamathas, the Uttaradi, Vyasaraya and Raghavendra Mathas are also centres of the Madhva principles (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 16, PDF p. 88).

**Exam Fact:** Ramanuja called the untouchables "Thirukulattar" and gave all devotees temple entry irrespective of birth (II PUC History, Ch 6, PDF p. 167).

text:
Arrange the following military events of Mughal history in chronological order:
1. First Battle of Panipat – Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi
2. Battle of Haldighati – Akbar's forces clash with Rana Pratap of Mewar
3. Conquest of Bijapur – Aurangzeb annexes the Adilshahi sultanate
4. Battle of Karnal – Nadir Shah defeats emperor Muhammad Shah
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
a) 1-3-2-4
b) 1-2-3-4
c) 4-3-2-1
d) 2-1-4-3
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
The correct sequence is 1-2-3-4:
- **1. First Battle of Panipat, 1526:** Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 (NCERT Class 8, Exploring Society Part 1, Ch 2, p. 36).
- **2. Battle of Haldighati, 1576:** the confrontation between the Mughal army and Maharana Pratap took place at the Haldighati pass in the Aravallis in 1576 (NCERT Class 8, Exploring Society Part 1, Ch 2, p. 47).
- **3. Conquest of Bijapur, 1686:** Bijapur fell in 1686 after an 18-month siege, with Aurangzeb personally present in its final stages (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 185).
- **4. Battle of Karnal, 1739:** Nadir Shah's expedition against the Mughal Empire came in 1739 (DSERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 43), and the Mughal army was defeated at Karnal (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 269).

**Option (a): Incorrect.** 1-3-2-4 places the conquest of Bijapur (1686) before Haldighati (1576).
**Option (b): Correct.** 1-2-3-4 runs 1526, 1576, 1686, 1739.
**Option (c): Incorrect.** 4-3-2-1 is the reverse of the true order.
**Option (d): Incorrect.** 2-1-4-3 places Haldighati before Panipat and Karnal before Bijapur.
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** Panipat (1526), Haldighati (1576), Bijapur (1686) and Karnal (1739) run in that order, 1-2-3-4.

**Salient Features: The four battles**
The four events run from the founding of Mughal rule under Babur to its humbling by Nadir Shah.
- **Babur's guns:** the battle at Panipat relied heavily on gunpowder, field artillery and matchlock guns (NCERT Class 8, Exploring Society Part 1, Ch 2, p. 36).
- **The Second Battle of Panipat, 1556:** it was fought between Hemu and the Mughals and was Akbar's decisive victory (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 5; NCERT Class 8, Exploring Society Part 1, Ch 2, p. 23).
- **Rana Pratap:** a huge bronze statue of Rana Pratap riding his horse Chetak was erected at Haldighat after Independence (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 15, p. 68).
- **After Karnal:** the defeat was followed by the death of the Mir Bakhshi, Khan-i-Dauran, the capture of Nizam-ul-Mulk and Saadat Khan, and the surrender of the Mughal emperor (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 269).

**Exam Fact:** Nadir Shah rose to power by leading a Persian war of resistance against the Afghans, and then ascended the throne of Persia (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 268).

text:
"Vaddaradhane", a collection of Jain religious stories and a noteworthy Kannada prose work of the Rashtrakuta period, was written by
a) Shivakotiacharya
b) Nayasena
c) Durgasimha
d) Rudrabhatta
sol:
**Correct Option: (a)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Correct.** The author of Vaddaradhane, a noteworthy prose work of the Rashtrakuta period and a collection of Jain religious stories, is **Shivakotiacharya** (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 33; II PUC History, Ch 4.8, PDF p. 99).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Nayasena composed "Dharmamruta", in the period of the Chalukyas of Kalyana (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF pp. 36–37).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** Durgasimha wrote the "Panchatantra", in the period of the Chalukyas of Kalyana (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 36).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Rudrabhatta wrote "Jagannatha Vijaya", in the Hoysala period (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 21, PDF p. 43).
Hence the correct answer is option (a).

**Result:** Vaddaradhane is by Shivakotiacharya; Nayasena and Durgasimha wrote under the Kalyana Chalukyas and Rudrabhatta under the Hoysalas.

**Salient Features: Kannada and Sanskrit writing, Rashtrakutas to Hoysalas**
Each dynasty in turn patronised Kannada and Sanskrit authors.
- **Vaddaradhane's style:** it gives special importance to native Kannada words and shows liveliness in plot, structure, characterisation and dialogue (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 33).
- **Sanskrit under the Rashtrakutas:** the Rashtrakutas encouraged both Kannada and Sanskrit, and Trivikrama wrote the Sanskrit "Nalachampu" (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 33).
- **Kalyana Chalukya period:** Kannada literature prospered with the support of Jain scholars, and vachana literature was the unique contribution of the period (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF pp. 36–37).
- **Hoysala period:** Keshiraja wrote the "Shabdamani Darpana" (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 21, PDF p. 43).

**Exam Fact:** The Rashtrakuta kings were devotees of Shiva and Vishnu, while Jainism received royal patronage and became a widespread religion (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 20, PDF p. 34).

text:
Which one of the following statements about monuments of the Deccan sultanates is NOT correct?
a) The Hafta Gumbaz, a complex of seven tombs, is at Vijayapura.
b) The Vijayapura fort has 96 bastions and six main entrances.
c) The Shah Bazaar mosque is at Kalaburagi.
d) The Solah Khamba mosque stands within the Bidar fort.
sol:
**Correct Option: (a)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Correct.** The statement is NOT correct, so it is the answer. The Hafta Gumbaz, a seven-tomb complex, is at **Gulbarga (Kalaburagi)**, not Vijayapura (II PUC History, Ch 5.5, PDF p. 161).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** The statement is correct. The Vijayapura fort is a massive structure with 96 bastions (towers) and six main entrances (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 65).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** The statement is correct. The Shah Bazaar mosque is among the monuments at Gulbarga (Kalaburagi) (II PUC History, Ch 5.5, PDF p. 161).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** The statement is correct. DSERT names the Solahkhamb mosque together with the palaces in the fort of Bidar (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 63), and II PUC lists the Solha Khamba mosque among the monuments of Bidar (II PUC History, Ch 5.5, PDF p. 161).
Hence the correct answer is option (a).

**Result:** The Hafta Gumbaz and the Shah Bazaar mosque are at Kalaburagi; the 96-bastion fort is at Vijayapura and the Solah Khamba mosque at Bidar.

**Salient Features: The Deccani style of architecture**
The sultanates built forts, mosques, palaces and tombs in a style of their own.
- **Dakhani style:** the buildings at Kalaburagi, Bidar and other places combined Indo-Islamic styles, and this style came to be known as the Dakhani style (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 63).
- **Main features:** tall minarets, strong arches, huge domes, spacious hazaras (big halls) and a crescent moon at the top, built with local materials (II PUC History, Ch 5.5, PDF p. 161).
- **Bidar palaces:** the Rangeen Mahal, Court Mahal, Janata Mahal and Janana Mahal are among the Bidar monuments (II PUC History, Ch 5.5, PDF p. 161).
- **Kalaburagi tombs:** there are tombs with huge domes near Kalaburagi, and the tomb of the Sufi saint Bandenawaz is another important structure (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 63).

**Exam Fact:** The language used by foreign scholars at the Bahmani court came to be known as Dakhani, which later led to the development of Urdu (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 63).

text:
Consider the following statements about the Vijayanagara period:
1. The Kamal Mahal and the elephant stables at Hampi are examples of the Indo-Muslim style.
2. Granite was used in the construction of buildings.
3. Lepakshi is called the Ajanta of Vaishnavism.
4. Sasivekalu Ganesha and Kadalekalu Ganesha are monolithic idols at Hampi.

How many of the above statements are correct?
a) Only one
b) Only two
c) Only three
d) All four
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** The Kamal Mahal, the elephant stable and the queen's bath at Hampi are examples of the Indo-Muslim architectural style (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 53).
**Statement 2: Correct.** During the Vijayanagara period, granite was used in the construction of buildings (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 56; II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 151).
**Statement 3: Incorrect.** Lepakshi is called the **"Ajanta of Shaivism"**, not of Vaishnavism; the paintings of the Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi relate to Shaiva mythology (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 152).
**Statement 4: Correct.** Sasivekalu Ganesha, Kadalekalu Ganesha and Lakshminarasimha are the monolithic idols at Hampi (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 58).
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, so three statements are correct, which is option (c).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Three statements are correct; Lepakshi is the Ajanta of Shaivism, not of Vaishnavism.

**Salient Features: Vijayanagara art beyond the capital**
Vijayanagara art and architecture spread well beyond Hampi.
- **Temples and basadis:** the Vidyashankara temple of Sringeri and the Thousand-pillared basadi of Mudabidri (Tribhuvana Tilaka Chudamani) belong to the Vijayanagara period (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 57).
- **Bahubali statues:** the monolithic statues of Bahubali at Karkala and Venur belong to this period (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, PDF p. 58).
- **Painting centres:** Hampi, Anegondi and Lepakshi were centres of Vijayanagara painting; the marriage of Pampamba with Virupaksha, Madana Vijaya and Tripura Samhara are among the great paintings (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 152).
- **Sangeeta Mantapas:** halls for music, dance and drama were built within temple premises (II PUC History, Ch 5.4, PDF p. 151).

**Exam Fact:** The fort of Hampi had seven circular walls, of which only four remain today (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, Ch 4, PDF p. 53).

text:
Which Kannada theatre personality, whose troupe 'Gubbi Veeranna Nataka Company' gave an early platform to several future film stars including Dr. Rajkumar, is regarded as a pioneer of professional Kannada theatre?
a) B.V. Karanth
b) Gubbi Veeranna
c) T.P. Kailasam
d) Chittani Ramachandra Hegde
sol:
**Correct Option: (b)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** B.V. Karanth belongs to amateur theatre: the Handbook records that when the need for a capable director was felt, talented directors like him came into the limelight (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 975). He did not found the Gubbi company.
**Option (b): Correct.** DSERT records that the name of Gubbi Veeranna has remained eternal in the history of Karnataka theatre; he bore the titles 'Natakarathna' and 'Nataka Sarvabhouma' and belonged to Gubbi in Tumkur district (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 28). The Handbook cites H.K. Ranganath for the view that, in the last decade of the 19th century, Veeranna's Gubbi Company had the credit of establishing the Kannada stage in South India (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 974).
**Option (c): Incorrect.** T.P. Kailasam is named among the pioneers of the modern Kannada play and among the great amateur artists (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 139); he did not found a professional company.
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Chittani Ramachandra Heggade received the Janapada Sri Award, which is given for outstanding service in folklore, in 2003 (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 933). He belongs to the folk tradition, not to company drama.
Hence the correct answer is option (b).

**Result:** Gubbi Veeranna, whose Gubbi company toured the state and who was titled 'Natakarathna', is the pioneer of professional Kannada theatre; Kailasam and Karanth belong to amateur theatre and Chittani to folk art.

**Salient Features: Professional theatre in Karnataka**
In the late nineteenth century professional drama troupes began touring the state and performing at different centres (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 974).
- **The early companies:** the Gazetteer lists the Karnataka Nataka Mandali of Gadag (c. 1874), the Palace Troupe (1881), the Rajadhani Nataka Mandali (1881), the Gubbi Company (1884) and the Tantupurusha Nataka Mandali of Dharwad (1885) (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 358).
- **The Gubbi Veeranna Award:** established in 1994 and considered the highest theatre award, it is given by the Department of Kannada and Culture (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 978).
- **Into cinema:** with Devudu Narasimha Sastri and Algod of Belagavi, Gubbi Veeranna helped set up the 'Karnataka Pictures Corporation', which produced silent films (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 989).
- **The first talkie:** DSERT names Subbaiah Naidu as the hero of the first Kannada talkie, 'Sathi Sulochana' (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 28).

**Exam Fact:** The first Dr. Gubbi Veeranna Award went to Enagi Balappa in 1994, and B.V. Karanth received it in 1995 (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 978).

text:
Match the Gupta-era monument in List I with its location in List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Dashavatara Temple | I. Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh |
| B. Bhitargaon Temple (brick temple) | II. Deogarh, Uttar Pradesh |
| C. Temple No. 17 | III. Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh |
| D. Udayagiri Caves | IV. Near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh |

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
a) A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV
b) A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
c) A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV
d) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
The correct matching is **A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV**.
- **A-II:** NCERT pictures a Gupta-era temple at Deogarh, Uttar Pradesh, c. fifth century CE (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 106), and the relief of Vishnu on Sheshnag from the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 162).
- **B-III:** the brick temple of Bhitargaon is one of the Gupta temples (II PUC History, Ch 4, PDF p. 73); it stands near Kanpur in Uttar Pradesh.
- **C-I:** Temple No. 17 is the Gupta-era temple near Sanchi, in Madhya Pradesh (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 163).
- **D-IV:** the Udayagiri Caves, with their rock-cut carvings of deities, are also in Madhya Pradesh (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 163), near Vidisha.

**Option (a): Incorrect.** It gets A-II and D-IV right but exchanges the middle rows, sending the brick temple to Sanchi (B-I) and Temple No. 17 to Kanpur (C-III).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** It gets B-III and C-I right but exchanges the Dashavatara temple and the Udayagiri Caves (A-IV, D-II).
**Option (c): Correct.** It gives A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.
**Option (d): Incorrect.** It gets B-III and D-IV right but exchanges the Dashavatara temple and Temple No. 17 (A-I, C-II).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** The Dashavatara temple is at Deogarh, the brick temple at Bhitargaon near Kanpur, Temple No. 17 at Sanchi and the Udayagiri Caves near Vidisha.

**Salient Features: Gupta temples and art**
DSERT dates the development of temple architecture in India to the times of the Guptas (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 16).
- **The early temple:** it was a small square room, the garbhagriha, with a single doorway for the worshipper; gradually a tall structure, the shikhara, was built over the central shrine (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, pp. 105–106).
- **Terracotta river goddesses:** Gupta-period terracotta sculptures from Ahichchhatra in western Uttar Pradesh show Ganga standing on a makara and Yamuna on a tortoise (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 162).
- **The iron pillar:** the 6-tonne pillar was erected in the reign of Chandragupta II, was probably first set up in front of the Udayagiri caves and was brought to Delhi a few centuries later; it was dedicated to Vishnu (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 148).
- **Other Gupta works:** II PUC names the Shiva temple of Bhumara among the Gupta temples, and the Sultanganj Buddha, 7½ feet high, now in the museum at Birmingham (II PUC History, Ch 4, PDF p. 73).

**Exam Fact:** The Ajanta murals were painted with locally available colours and ordinary brushes, and the caves, hidden from view for many centuries, were discovered in 1819 (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 20).

text:
Consider the following statements:
1. Kalidasa, honoured with the title 'Kavikula Guru', is the author of the play 'Abhijnana Shakuntalam'.
2. Shudraka's Sanskrit play 'Mrichakatika' ('The Little Clay Cart') is a social drama centred on a merchant's love for a courtesan.
3. Vishakhadatta's play 'Mudrarakshasa' dramatises the political intrigue behind Chandragupta Maurya's rise to power.
Which of the above statements are correct?
a) 1 and 2 only
b) 1 and 3 only
c) 2 and 3 only
d) 1, 2 and 3
sol:
**Correct Option: (d)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** Kalidasa has been hailed as 'Kavikula Guru', and 'Abhijnana Shakunthalam' is his great play (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 16).
**Statement 2: Correct.** Shudraka wrote the 'Mricchakatika' (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 16). Its hero Charudatta is described as both a Brahmana and a sarthavaha, or merchant (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 3, p. 64), and the play turns on his love for the courtesan Vasantasena, a story of townspeople rather than of gods or kings.
**Statement 3: Correct.** Vishakhadatta wrote the 'Mudrarakshasa' (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 16; DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, p. 8). The play turns on Chanakya's manoeuvres to win over Rakshasa, the minister of the Nandas, for Chandragupta Maurya.
Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, which is option (d). Option (a) omits the true 3; option (b) omits the true 2; option (c) omits the true 1.
Hence the correct answer is option (d).

**Result:** Kalidasa ('Kavikula Guru') wrote Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Shudraka the social drama Mricchakatika and Vishakhadatta the political drama Mudrarakshasa.

**Salient Features: Kalidasa and the Sanskrit drama**
DSERT records that Kalidasa composed four epics and three dramas (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 16).
- **His plays and poems:** the plays are Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Malavikagnimitra and Vikramorvashiya; the poems are Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava, Ritusamhara and Meghaduta (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 18).
- **The story of Shakuntala:** it comes from the Mahabharata; King Dushyanta meets Shakuntala at Sage Kanva's ashram, and Sage Durvasa's curse makes him forget her (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, p. 8).
- **Shakuntala in English:** William Jones translated 'Shakuntala' into English (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 14).
- **The theory of drama:** the Natyashastra of Bharata is a Sanskrit work on dramaturgy (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 3, p. 79).

**Exam Fact:** In the Shakuntala story the lost ring is found in the stomach of a fish, and on seeing it Dushyanta recalls everything (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, p. 8).

text:
The title 'Kannada-rajya-ramaramana' belonged to which of the following rulers?
a) Vikramaditya VI
b) Hoysala Vishnuvardhana
c) Krishnadevaraya
d) Pulakeshi II
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** Vikramaditya VI was a king of the Chalukyas of Kalyana, and II PUC gives his titles as 'Permadideva' and 'Tribhuvanamalla' (II PUC History, Ch 4.9, PDF p. 103). 'Kannada-rajya-ramaramana' is not his title.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Vishnuvardhana was a Hoysala king; the Handbook mentions his queen Shantaladevi, praised in inscriptions as an expert in dance (Handbook of Karnataka 2020, p. 988). 'Kannada-rajya-ramaramana' is not his title.
**Option (c): Correct.** DSERT states that the title of Krishnadevaraya was "Kannada-rajya-ramaramana" (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 14, p. 51).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Pulakeshi II bore the titles 'Dakshinapatheshwara' and 'Lord of the Peninsula' (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 19, p. 22).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** 'Kannada-rajya-ramaramana' was Krishnadevaraya's title; Pulakeshi II was 'Dakshinapatheshwara', and Vikramaditya VI bore the titles 'Permadideva' and 'Tribhuvanamalla'.

**Salient Features: Titles of Karnataka's rulers**
Rulers of Karnataka's dynasties took titles that recorded victories, piety or claims to rule.
- **Pulakeshi I:** he had titles like Satyashraya and Vallabha, and he called himself Dharmamaharaja (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, PDF p. 73).
- **Pulakeshi II:** he assumed the title Parameshwara (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 64), and he also bore titles like Satyashraya, Prithveevallabha and Dakshinapatha Prithveeswamy (Kamath, p. 65).
- **Taila II:** after defeating Chaulukya Mularaja of Gujarat he assumed the title Gurjarabhayajvara; Satyashrayakulatilaka and Nurmaditaila were his other titles (Kamath, p. 106).
- **Harihara II:** the work of writing commentaries on the Vedas was completed in his days, and he assumed the title Vaidikamarga Sthapanacharya (Kamath, p. 172).

**Exam Fact:** Pulakeshi II was also known as Ereya (Kamath, *A Concise History of Karnataka*, p. 64).

text:
Consider the following statements about Bodhisattvas in Buddhism:
1. In Mahayana belief, a Bodhisattva is a compassionate being who gathers merit but, instead of attaining nirvana and leaving the world, uses it to help others.
2. Maitreya is the Bodhisattva regarded as the future Buddha.
3. The famous Padmapani painting at Ajanta depicts Bodhisattva Manjushri.
Which of the above statements are correct?
a) 1 and 2 only
b) 2 and 3 only
c) 1 and 3 only
d) 1, 2 and 3
sol:
**Correct Option: (a)**

**Justification:**
**Statement 1: Correct.** Bodhisattas were perceived as deeply compassionate beings who accumulated merit through their efforts but used it not to attain nibbana and thereby abandon the world, but to help others; this new way of thinking was called Mahayana (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 103).
**Statement 2: Correct.** Maitreya is the Bodhisattva who, in Buddhist belief, is to come as the future Buddha; NCERT illustrates a Kushana-period image of Bodhisattva Maitreya (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 141).
**Statement 3: Incorrect.** The famous Ajanta painting is of Bodhisattva Padmapani (NCERT Class 7, Exploring Society Part 1, p. 163). Padmapani, "lotus in hand", is a form of Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of compassion, whom the Ajanta artists depicted in painting and sculpture (Tamil Nadu Class 11 History, p. 152). Manjushri is a different Bodhisattva.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct, which is option (a). Option (b) includes the false 3 and omits 1; option (c) includes the false 3 and omits 2; option (d) includes the false 3.
Hence the correct answer is option (a).

**Result:** Bodhisattvas use their merit to help others and Maitreya is the future Buddha, but the Ajanta Padmapani is Avalokiteshvara, not Manjushri.

**Salient Features: Bodhisattvas and Mahayana**
NCERT traces how, alongside the older view of the Buddha as a human teacher, the idea of a saviour gradually emerged (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 103).
- **Self-effort first:** early Buddhist teachings had given great importance to self-effort in achieving nibbana, and the Buddha was regarded as a human being who attained it through his own efforts; by the first century CE there is evidence of change (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 103).
- **Images:** the worship of images of the Buddha and the Bodhisattas became an important part of the Mahayana tradition (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 103).
- **Gandhara:** images of the Buddha and Bodhisattas evidently based on Greek models were found mostly in the north-west, in cities such as Taxila and Peshawar (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 108).
- **Karnataka:** the Kadri Manjunatha temple at Mangaluru has a huge bronze statue of Avalokiteshvara, about a thousand years old (DSERT Class 7 Social Science Part 1, 2026-27, p. 101), and the Gazetteer notes that Buddhist centres such as Kadri later turned to Shaiva worship, Manjushri becoming Manjunatha (Karnataka Gazetteer 1982, Part 1, p. 423).

**Exam Fact:** An inscription of the year 33 of the Kushana ruler Huvishka records that the bhikkhuni Dhanavati set up an image of a Bodhisatta at Madhuvanaka (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part I, Ch 4, p. 111).

text:
Which of the following methods of assessing Mughal land revenue involved actual division of the harvested crop between the state and the cultivator, rather than a cash assessment based on measurement?
a) Nasaq
b) Zabti
c) Batai (Ghalla-Bakshi)
d) Dahsala
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** The nature of nasaq is debated: Moreland called it group assessment, while Irfan Habib considers it an estimation based on the previous assessment, whether that had been made by zabt, batai or another method (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 84). On either reading it is not a physical division of the harvest.
**Option (b): Incorrect.** Zabt was the system of measurement adopted by Sher Shah and continued under Akbar (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 81); bamboo measuring sticks with iron hooks were used to measure the land (DSERT Class 9 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, p. 7).
**Option (c): Correct.** The Ain describes batai, also called bhaoli, in which the crops are reaped and stacked and divided by agreement in the presence of the parties (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 8, p. 215). Satish Chandra lists this crop-sharing in three types: bhaoli, khet batai (the fields divided after they were sown) and lang batai (the cut grain formed into heaps and divided) (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 84).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** Under the dahsala, the Ten-Year rates proclaimed in 1579, the state demand was expressed as a cash rate based on local productivity and local prices (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 82). It is a cash assessment, not a division of the crop.
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Batai divided the harvested crop between the state and the cultivator; zabt and dahsala fixed a cash demand on measured land, and nasaq worked from earlier assessments.

**Salient Features: Assessing land revenue under Akbar**
The Ain lists several methods of assessment and collection in use side by side (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 8, p. 215).
- **Classes of land:** polaj was cultivated every year and never left fallow; parauti was left out of cultivation for a time to recover; chachar had lain fallow for three or four years; banjar was uncultivated for five years and more (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 8, p. 214).
- **Kankut:** in Hindi, kan means grain and kut estimate; under kankut the crop was estimated, and in case of doubt cut and estimated in three lots, good, middling and inferior (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 8, p. 215).
- **Where zabt ran:** the dahsala system based on measurement was introduced from Lahore to Allahabad and in Gujarat, Malwa and parts of Bihar and Multan, though Irfan Habib thinks it improbable that zabt covered the whole land in any province (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 83).
- **Kashmir:** there the produce was computed in ass-loads (kharwar) and then divided (Satish Chandra, Medieval India Part II, PDF p. 84).

**Exam Fact:** According to the Ain, the produce of the three classes of land was averaged, and one-third of this medium produce was exacted as the royal dues (NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History Part II, Ch 8, p. 214).

text:
The monastic university of Nalanda was set up in the
a) third century BCE
b) second century BCE
c) fifth century CE
d) eighth century CE
sol:
**Correct Option: (c)**

**Justification:**
**Option (a): Incorrect.** The third century BCE is far too early. Nalanda was set up in the fifth century CE (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 146).
**Option (b): Incorrect.** The second century BCE is also too early for the same reason (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 146).
**Option (c): Correct.** Nalanda was set up in the **fifth century**, and its earliest structure, made of brick, belongs to this period (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 146). Its buildings were raised and renovated over some 700 years from the fifth century AD (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 155).
**Option (d): Incorrect.** By the eighth century Nalanda was long established: the Chinese pilgrim Hsuan Tsang, who left China in AD 629, came to study at the Buddhist university of Nalanda (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 154).
Hence the correct answer is option (c).

**Result:** Nalanda was set up in the fifth century CE, from which its earliest brick structure dates.

**Salient Features: Nalanda as a monastic university**
Nalanda was a great Buddhist university meant for Buddhist monks (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 155).
- **Teaching:** it taught the Buddhist philosophy of the Mahayana school and is said to have had as many as 10,000 students, all monks (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 155).
- **Excavations:** they have exposed a very impressive complex of buildings, though the buildings exposed so far could not have housed 10,000 monks (R.S. Sharma, Ancient India, p. 155).
- **Campus:** there were stupas, chaityas, viharas, rest houses, meditation rooms and lecture rooms (DSERT Class 8 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 17, PDF p. 14).
- **Copper Buddha:** an 8-foot copper statue of the Buddha from Gupta times stands at Nalanda (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 20).

**Exam Fact:** Although Buddhism was the main subject of study at Nalanda, the Vedas, Yoga, medicine and other subjects were also taught there (DSERT Class 6 Social Science Part 2, 2026-27, Ch 12, PDF p. 25).
